public_rationale: OpenAI acknowledged on March 14, 2023 that GPT-4 could still produce unsafe behavior, but this establishes limitations of one model [e1]. The February 12, 2024 erase-and-check paper gives guarantees for bounded prompt attacks, conditional on a filter detecting the original harmful prompt [e2]. The November 28, 2023 robot paper describes enforcement of human-verified constraints, with assumptions about state predicates and a transition model [e3]. These candidates show narrower guarantees, but the records do not establish safety assurance covering the relevant hazards of their intended use [e2, e3]. The evidence therefore establishes neither a qualifying counterexample nor that no qualifying system existed by February 21, 2024 [e1–e3].
limitations: The evidence covers selected systems and methods, not a comprehensive history of safety assurance.
The candidate records do not establish adequate hazard coverage and justified operating assumptions for system-level safety assurance.
The claim leaves the required hazards and operating scope unspecified. This assessment concerns achievements by February 21, 2024.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: No one has ever been able to engineer safety guarantees for generative AI systems.

statement.excerpt: Nobody has ever been able to engineer safety guarantees around then.

our_interpretation: Read “then” as a typographical error for “them,” referring to the generative AI systems discussed in the post.
The plain reading is that nobody had engineered meaningful assurance that these systems would behave safely in their intended use by February 21, 2024.

A qualifying guarantee must address the safety of the functioning system within a stated operating scope. Reasonable operating assumptions are acceptable; freedom from every conceivable harm is not required.
A certificate for one attack mechanism or component does not by itself establish the system-level assurance described in the claim. Its coverage and assumptions must be examined.
“Ever” covers the history preceding publication, so the target period has no specified starting date. This is not a forecast that safety guarantees will remain impossible.
criteria.support_condition: A sufficiently comprehensive technical assessment of the field as it stood by February 21, 2024 establishes that meaningful system-level safety assurance had not been engineered, addressing credible candidate systems and the limitations of their guarantees.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A documented system engineered by February 21, 2024 demonstrably provides meaningful assurance of safe behavior in its intended operating scope, with justified assumptions and coverage of the relevant hazards. An isolated conditional certificate is insufficient without evidence connecting it to that assurance.

evidence.explanation: OpenAI acknowledged that its interventions did not prevent all bad behavior in GPT-4. This is consistent with Marcus's concern, but one model's limitations cannot establish that nobody had engineered qualifying assurance.

evidence.locator: Introduction, paragraph introducing erase-and-check; scope explained under adversarial attack modes
evidence.explanation: This is a genuine candidate against an unrestricted reading of “safety guarantees.” Its certificate concerns bounded token additions and depends on the original harmful prompt being detected by the safety filter; it does not establish overall safe behavior.

evidence.excerpt: The human specifies safety constraints in English.
evidence.locator: Section III-B, Overview; assumptions in Sections III-A, III-E, and V-A
evidence.explanation: The proposed safety module enforces human-verified formal constraints around an LLM-driven robot, making it a more relevant candidate than a prompt certificate alone. Its assurance assumes perfect state predicates and a transition model; the examined evidence does not establish coverage of the hazards needed for the broader assurance meant here.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A documented system engineered by February 21, 2024 with verified safety assurance covering relevant hazards in its intended operating scope, under justified assumptions, would contradict the claim. A comprehensive historical technical assessment establishing that no qualifying assurance existed by that date, including examination of credible candidates, would support it.
